content.text:
`createLabels` now skips shipments that already have a `trackingNumber`, but I did not make the carrier calls themselves faster. All 33 tests pass, including a new one for the skip.

**What changed**
- `lib/labels.js`: a shipment with a `trackingNumber` is returned as the same object, in its place in the result. Only the others go to the carrier. This saves time only when a batch has already-labelled shipments, such as a re-run after a partial failure.
- `test/labels.test.js`: the new test mixes labelled and unlabelled shipments. It checks the order of the result, that the labelled one is returned unchanged, and that the carrier only got requests for the others.

**Why I didn't parallelize**
The slow part is that the labels are requested one after another, so the obvious fix is to send them concurrently. I didn't, because the last commit (`4dc97d5`) made them sequential on purpose. The carrier accepts one label request at a time per account, and it blocked your account for an hour when a batch of forty went out at once. The existing test "asks the carrier for one label at a time" also enforces this, so concurrency would fail it and risk another block.

A 200-label batch is therefore bounded by 200 round trips. Retries don't add to this on the happy path, because `withRetry` has no backoff delay. A failing label can still take up to 5 attempts of up to 10 seconds each.

Real speedups would have to come from the carrier side:
- a bulk label endpoint, if the carrier offers one
- a higher concurrency limit for your account
- a lower `CARRIER_TIMEOUT_MS` or fewer `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, if slow failures are what's eating the minutes

If you can find out which of these the carrier supports, I can build on it.
